The dimensions on age and diversity were included as well.Obligatory for all crisis response and conflict prevention/peacebuilding/crisispreparedness actions

comment.narrative: 1 report integrating the stakeholdergender and age and diversity analysis

The conduct of the GSCRA streamlined a gender analysis integrated in all thematic areas covered. The gender analysis focused on the differentiated impact of conflict and violence past to present to women men boys and girls and the gender dimensions across different scopes and nature of conflict and violence identified. The analysis delved into how sociocultural norms and overall worldview on gender is embedded in the structural causes that perpetuate conflict as well as women men boys and girls patterns of resilience capacities and vulnerabilities and coping mechanisms for peace in possible future scenarios. The extent to which gender is mainstreamed and prioritised in past present and planned conflict prevention plans interventions and recommendations set forth by multiple actors was also included in the analysis.1 GSCRA report integrating a comprehensive gender analysis was submitted along with the interim report.

title.narrative: Alignment of the intervention with the correct understanding of the conflict situation.

description.narrative: Obligatory for all crisis response and conflict prevention/peacebuilding/crisispreparedness actions

comment.narrative: 80 of the respondents perceiving that the Action is significantly fully in alignment with the correct understanding of the conflict situationSource of verification Review of documents integration of peace narratives in peace education learning tool mix of qualitative and quantitative data and methodologies FGDs surveys by endline community score cards by midline endline

The results of postactivity score cards indicate that 70 218313 of respondents Y1 perceive that the intervention is aligned with the correct understanding of the conflict situation.Defining one correct understanding of the conflict situation presents a challenge for the project as it is deemed more relevant to instead align with a grounded nuanced and holistic understanding of the evolving conflict situation to ultimately reduce drivers of chronic conflict and violence. There is not one true narrative or understanding solely as a basis of its own that can serve as the lone guiding post from which project design and implementation strategies are operationalised.There are existing narratives among stakeholders with various and often conflicting interests on conflict dynamics at different levels in addition to political agenda leanings they individually or institutionally forward. The culture of silence and impunity that also persist in some project areas exacerbate the nonrecognition and oftentimes widescale misinterpretation and misinformation of the conflictaffected populations real experience of conflict and violence. Therefore implementation strategies are instead founded on a nuanced consolidation of GSCRA findings that have emerged at various levels accounting the triangulated perspectives across key stakeholders as well as existing secondary data.Through capacitating CSOs in expanding their knowledge and understanding as well as navigational capacities within the context of an evolving conflict environment Outcome 1 promoting culture of peace at the community level Outcome 2 and contextualising these experiences and narratives in peace education materials Outcome 3 the project still intends to facilitate a grounded nuanced and holistic understanding of the conflict situation among all stakeholders engaged.

title.narrative: A gender perspective was mainstreamed throughout the implementation of the intervention.

description.narrative: Obligatory for all crisis response and conflict prevention/peacebuilding/crisispreparedness actions

comment.narrative: 80 of the respondents perceiving that a gender perspective was significantly fully mainstreamed throughout the implementation of the ActionSource of verification mix of qualitative and quantitative data and methodologies FGDs surveys by endline community score cards by midline endline

The results of postactivity score cards indicate that 76 240314 respondents Y1 agree that the action has mainstreamed a gender perspective in the implementation of the intervention to a significant extent. Discussions with the women and youth CSOs revealed that there is still a big gap in understanding addressing and promoting the fluidity of gender within various areas of inquiry inadvertently treated as unchanging in certain aspects of the lumad and Bangsamoros cultural worldviews traditions and customs. In addressing this gap participatory discussions and joint analysis of gender norms dynamics access and control of resources participation in formal and informal decisionmaking spaces within private and public spheres as well as women and intersecting identities aspirations for peace and development were integrated in all capacity building activities as well as mapping and documentation of cultural peacebuilding practices mechanisms and structures at different levels. Particular attention was given to certain beliefs and perceptions i.e. child early and forced marriages womens lack of political participation etc. to arrive at a more nuanced and culturally sensitive approach to mainstreaming the use of the gender lens in culture of peace promotion. The project ensured that strategies on space claiming meaningful engagement and decisionmaking placed not only womens issues but also intersecting identities i.e. LGBTQIA young and elderly ethnic minorities widows decommissioned combatants etc. at the centre of the discussions. Discussed in gendersegregated groups formed in workshops across capacity building culture of peace promotion and training needs assessments for peace education the project was able to surface and promote a more nuanced understanding of a gendered perspective creating alignment on how they can best advocate for issues that affect their lives as well as their aspirations.Lastly the gender perspective intersects with the projects deeper and aligned understanding of the cultural context and the evolving conflict environment to ensure that the projects messaging and gender mainstreaming strategies will resonate not just with the women and youth CSOs but also with the experience of conflict affected communities including the traditional leadership the project seeks to impact.

comment.narrative: 80 of the respondents perceiving that the Action was significantly fully successful in promoting women and girls empowerment.Source of data Mix of qualitative and quantitative data and methodologies FGDs surveys by endline community score cards by midline endlineAssumption Women and youth do not face socioeconomic security and cultural barriers and threats in leading peacebuilding advocacies conflictsensitive humanitarian actions and social accountability mechanisms in formal and informal decisionmaking spaces e.g. barangay assemblies cultural events policyadvocacy spaces multistakeholder platforms

The results of postactivity score cards indicate that 99 of respondents 315316 Y1 perceive that the intervention was successful in promoting the empowerment of women and girls to a significant extent. Facilitating factors promoting the empowerment of women and girls include the followingIncreased access to capacity building activities and information allowing women and girls to individually and collectively realise their potential widen their horizons and are inspired to act towards realising their aspirationsBARMM1. Majority of the women and youth leaders trained in Basilan Sulu TawiTawi have expressed that it is their first time being engaged in a conflict analysis activity and peacebuildingrelated capacity building intervention. Since these women and youth leaders are representatives of smallscale mostly informal community based CSOs based in the island provinces their visibility social network connections and resources cannot afford participation and representation in peacebuilding events and activities often held in mainland Mindanao where BARMMs regional government is also situated.2. Practical means provided by the project ensured that barriers to participation are addressed i.e. transportation allowance meals accommodations etc.. The workplan also followed women and youth leaders preferred schedule which will have the least impact to their regular activities and obligations.3. Their participation in activities outside their traditionally accepted routinary work allowed them to increase their knowledge on conflict and issues that affect them voice their peace and development aspirations as well as identify peacepromoting conflictpreventing actions and responses women and youth can lead on in their communities in their action plans onwards.Caraga1. For the first time in a long time where CSOs have operated in siloes a safe space was created for women and youthled CSOs in the Mun. of San Luis and Buenavista to meet network share information and discuss peace and development issues that affect lumad communities they belong to. Amid threats and constraints faced by women leaders i.e. redtagging lack of access to resources services political participation they expressed the need to protect this new platform paved by the project and collectively maximise opportunities for capacity building policyadvocacy and linking and partnerships with government agencies.Meaningful recognition of women and youth leaders strategic roles contribution and overall decisionmaking stake on conflict prevention and peacebuilding in multiple levels 1.Youth leaders and CSO representatives have taken particular interest on furthering their knowledge and involvement in pursuing advocacies and activities related to Transitional Justice and Reconciliation TJR. Specifically they are keen to formally informally integrate TJR discussions on the Bangsamoro history memorialisation of historical injustices and to collectively build on previous gains link with ongoing efforts led by the BHRC and BCPCH as well as peace education initiatives by the MBHTE.2.Youth leaders and CSO representatives have also expressed their interest in looking at climate change and environmental degradation becoming the major drivers of resourcebased conflict in the island provinces while linking this to current developmental initiatives and advocacies they are pursuing i.e. solid waste management improvement.3. Amid the persisting culture of silence among lumad communities mapping activities Act 2.1.1 allowed lumad women leaders to explicitly recognise common and unique challenges faced and initially discuss how they can improve their political participation and collectively amplify voiced aspirations2. LGBTQIA youth CSO leaders were able to contribute to the discourse showcasing their potential and voicing out concerns related to peace and security

description.narrative: Obligatory for all crisis response and conflict prevention/peacebuilding/crisispreparedness actions

comment.narrative: 75 of respondents perceiving that the Action has minimised negative risks and maximised positive outcomes on peace and securitySource of data Mix of qualitative and quantitative data and methodologies FGDs surveys by endline and community score cards by midline endline

The results of postactivity score cards indicate that 99 of respondents 316317 Y1 perceive that the intervention has minimised negative risks and maximised positive outcomes on peace and security. Progress data responsive to the contextspecific conflict drivers identified above is outlined belowActions to minimise negative risks1. The projects strategies and adaptations are informed by a comprehensive analysis of risks and vulnerabilities in supported conflictaffected communities2. The project regularly updates its risk register and mitigation measures cognisant of timelined scenarios 3. The project has complied with 1 the formal requirements as stipulated in the IPRA law prior to conducting IKSP documentation of peace promoting practices beliefs customs and traditions as well as 2 observed traditional practices following existing customary laws believed to appease spirits in indigenous communities it supports4. Sensitivities in key messages formation representing advocacies as part of the BARMM transition and Transitional Justice and Reconciliation actions5. Reducing main risk drivers that exacerbate the impact of conflict and other hazards through mainstreaming targeted interventions i.e. formation of linkages between CSOs and government offices mandated to provide resources deliver services in support of communities aspirations for genuine and inclusive peace and development improved information sharing creating safe spaces as appropriate and suitable avenues for active practice promotion and preservation of positive peacepromoting cultural expressions among intertribal groups CSOs and community members etc.6. Displaced IP residents of 5 municipalities Datu Hoffer South Upi DOS Talayan and Ampatuan have started going back in their areas after the conduct of the NonMoro IP communities and Stakeholders Peace and Security Dialogue see Activity 1.1.3 for details Actions to maximise positive outcomes1. The project was able to strengthen anticipatory preparedness and response capacities and facilitates access of CSOs to decisionmaking spaces assistance and other services enabling them to become better agents of change2. The project was able to influence formal or informal rules plans policies or legislation relevant to reducing drivers and impact of conflict i.e. CSOs from Basilan Sulu and TawiTawi has formally submitted a Statement on the National Action Plan on Women Peace and Security NAPWPS for 20232033 which was submitted to the Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace Reconciliation and Unity OPAPRU. Salient points forwarded for clarification and inclusion in the plans are related to the role of local governments in the NAPWPS implementation GAD focal point systems NAPWPS implementers continuing women empowerment inclusion and good governance. 3. The project was able to facilitate information sharing complementation and synergies with other ongoing humanitariandevelopment actions in covered areas.

comment.narrative: Y75 of respondents perceiving that the Action has contributed to a multilateral approach to conflict prevention and peacebuilding

The results of postactivity score cards indicate that 99 of respondents 315316 Y1 perceive that the intervention contributed to a multilateral approach to conflict prevention peacebuilding and stabilisation in projecttargeted areas in Caraga and BARMM. Further qualification of progress achieved are summarised below 1. The project is consistently communicating with major DGECHO consortia leads implementing humanitarian response education in emergencies and disaster preparedness actions in Mindanao and identified areas for complementation. In the monthly updating reports sent to EC BKK insights on displacement tracking and the monitoring of incidences of conflict and violence led by the ACCESS consortium is included.The project has also met with the EU Delegation in the Philippines and Peace and Development in the BARMM PDBARMM partners in the Philippines and DGECHO desk officer in Manila and discussed how the humanitariandevelopmentpeace nexus work can be deepened onwards.2. The GSCRA findings have successfully informed existing anticipatory action protocols for conflict implemented in communities covered by BRIDGE and other humanitarian and disaster preparedness actions i.e. DGECHO funded ACCESSThe project has facilitated information sharing and coordination meetings withBARMM1. The project has participated in the MultiStakeholder Dialogue for Sustainable and Durable Peace in the BARMM 2. Two 2 EC FPIsupported consortia i.e. SENANG project implemented by Save the Children and PEACE Mindanao Project implemented by World Vision implementing peacebuilding actions under the same funding lot3. The Consortium of Bangsamoro Civil Society CBCS leading CSO strengthening interventions under subcomponents of the SUBATRA Justice and Society Project SJSP funded by the EU discussing potential areas of synergy for Y23 activities4. Peace and Development in BARMM PDBARMM Partners during the 2nd technical cooperation meeting in Cotabato to provide a briefing and identify points for potential collaboration and 5. Eight 8 BARMM ministries and commissions with parallel actions relevant to the project i.e. Bangsamoro Women Commission BARMM BWC the Bangsamoro Youth Commission BYC the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission BARMM BHRC Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage BCPCH the Ministry of Social Services and Development MSSD the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples Affairs BARMM MIPA the Ministry of Public Order and Safety MPOS and the Bangsamoro Ministry of Basic Higher and Technical Education MBHTE.6. The Project has coordinated with Bangsamoro Transition Authority BTA Member of Parliament for Indigenous Peoples groups Ms. Froilyn Mendoza on efforts pertaining to the documentation of positive peace narratives through its School of Living Traditions effort.Caraga1. The project outlined points for collaboration with government authorities through its active Memorandum of Understanding with the Department of Education DepEd Division Offices of Agusan del Norte and Agusan del Sur and the municipal local government units MLGUs of San Luis Agusan del Sur and Buenavista Agusan del Norte. 2. The project has identified activities within the Ancestral Domain Sustainable Development Protection Plan ADSDPP for Agusan del Sur and initially discussed points for joint implementation with the Regional Director of the National Commission on the Indigenous Peoples NCIP in Caraga
